articleHeadline: When measles returns: The rare brain disease that can emerge years after infection
articleSummary: SSPE (subacute sclerosing panencephalitis) is a rare, progressive, usually fatal neurological disease caused by persistent measles infection. After a child recovers from measles—fever subsides and rash fades—years may pass before brain-related symptoms appear. Early signs include cognitive decline: forgetting lessons, loss of previously acquired skills, and behavioral changes, accompanied by worsening school performance. As SSPE progresses, frequent falls occur, followed by sudden jerking movements and seizures. Over time there is a gradual loss of movement, speech, and vision. The report highlights SSPE as a delayed consequence of measles infection, underscoring the long latency and severe outcome of this brain disease.

articleSummary: Leprosy (Hansen’s disease) in India has ancient roots. articleHeadline: Chikungunya Raises New Concerns Over Blood Transfusion Safety
articleSummary: Chikungunya (CHIKV), a mosquito-borne illness causing fever and severe joint pain, may threaten blood safety as outbreaks expand. The virus has been reported in more than 110 countries across Africa, Asia, the Americas, and Europe. Donors can be viremic even when asymptomatic: CHIKV RNA positivity around 0.5% overall, about 0.6% in endemic/outbreak settings, with higher rates of 1.9% in Puerto Rico and 1% in Thailand and French Polynesia. In Puerto Rico’s peak months, viral RNA was found in 1.34% of donors, with some very high viral loads. Lab studies show infectious CHIKV can survive routine blood processing, recovered from red cells, platelets, and plasma; however, this does not prove transmission. Clinically verified transfusion transmissions are extremely limited, so current risk is very low but not zero. Safeguards include NAAT screening and pathogen-reduction, not universally available. Italian institutions—Pisa, Rome’s Lazzaro Spallanzani, Mantua—contributed; findings published in Viruses.

articleHeadline: Flu risk rises for older adults during rainy season
articleSummary: Bangkok, Thailand—Influenza risk rises for adults aged 60+ with chronic illnesses during the rainy season, with potential pneumonia, heart failure, and prolonged hospitalization. Nationwide influenza cases exceeded 1 million in 2025; in the first half of 2026, more than 200,000 cases were reported with 25 deaths. Annual vaccination is vital, ideally before or during the rainy season to allow immunity development; combine with masks, handwashing, and avoiding crowds. For older adults, high-dose vaccines—four times the antigen of standard-dose vaccines—offer stronger protection. Clinical data cited by the Infectious Disease Association of Thailand show a 24.22% greater reduction in infections, 31.93% fewer influenza hospitalizations, 6.6% fewer hospitalizations for cardiovascular disease, and 21.3% fewer hospitalizations for heart failure. Options depend on age and health; older adults with chronic diseases should consult a doctor.
